content: Uveitis refers to a group of inflammatory diseases affecting the inside of the eye. It is the fifth leading cause of vision loss in high-income countries, particularly affecting individuals of working age. Corticosteroids are the primary treatment for all subtypes of non-infectious uveitis. These steroids can be delivered through various methods, including oral administration, topical eye drops, periocular injections (around the eye), intravitreal injections (inside the eye), or surgical implantation. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of corticosteroid implants in patients with chronic non-infectious posterior uveitis, intermediate uveitis, and panuveitis. The researchers conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials comparing fluocinolone acetonide (FA) or dexamethasone (DEX) intravitreal implants with standard-of-care therapy or sham procedures. The studies included participants of all ages with chronic non-infectious uveitis and vision better than hand motion. The follow-up period was at least six months. Four trials involving 683 participants and 907 eyes were included in the analysis. Two trials compared corticosteroid implants with sham procedures, one using a 0.18 mg FA implant and the other a 0.7 mg DEX implant. The other two trials compared a 0.59 mg FA implant with standard-of-care therapy, which included systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressive medications when necessary. The risk of bias in these trials was assessed as low or with some concerns. When compared to sham procedures, corticosteroid implants reduced the risk of uveitis recurrence by 60% at six months (relative risk [RR] 0.40, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.30 to 0.54; low-certainty evidence). They also improved best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) slightly (mean difference [MD] 0.15 logMAR, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.24; low-certainty evidence). However, evidence from a single study suggested that these implants had no significant effect on visual functioning quality of life, as measured by the National Eye Institute 25-Item Visual Function Questionnaire (MD 2.85, 95% CI -3.64 to 9.34; moderate-certainty evidence). When compared to standard-of-care therapy, corticosteroid implants reduced the risk of uveitis recurrence by 54% at 24 months (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.60). However, they had little to no effect on improving BCVA (MD 0.05 logMAR, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.12; low-certainty evidence). Evidence from a single study suggested minimal clinical effects on visual functioning (MD 4.64, 95% CI 0.13 to 9.15; moderate-certainty evidence), physical functioning (SF-36 physical subscale MD 2.95, 95% CI 0.55 to 5.35; moderate-certainty evidence), or mental health (SF-36 mental subscale MD 3.65, 95% CI 0.52 to 6.78; moderate-certainty evidence). There was no significant effect on EuroQoL scores (MD 6.17, 95% CI 1.87 to 10.47; moderate-certainty evidence) or the EuroQoL-5D scale (MD 0.02, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.08; moderate-certainty evidence). Regarding adverse effects, corticosteroid implants slightly increased the risk of cataract formation compared to sham procedures (RR 2.69, 95% CI 1.17 to 6.18; low-certainty evidence), but not the risk of cataract progression (RR 2.00, 95% CI 0.65 to 6.12; low-certainty evidence) or the need for cataract surgery (RR 2.98, 95% CI 0.82 to 10.81; low-certainty evidence) within 12 months of follow-up. The implants increased the risk of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) (RR 2.81, 95% CI 1.42 to 5.56; moderate-certainty evidence) and the need for IOP-lowering eye drops (RR 1.85, 95% CI 1.05 to 3.25; moderate-certainty evidence), but not the need for IOP-lowering surgery (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.13 to 4.17; moderate-certainty evidence). When compared to standard-of-care therapy, the 0.59 mg FA implant increased the risk of cataract progression (RR 2.71, 95% CI 2.06 to 3.56; low-certainty evidence) and the need for cataract surgery (RR 2.98, 95% CI 2.33 to 3.79; low-certainty evidence). It also increased the risk of elevated IOP (RR 3.64, 95% CI 2.71 to 4.87; moderate-certainty evidence) and the need for medical (RR 3.04, 95% CI 2.36 to 3.91; moderate-certainty evidence) or surgical interventions (RR 5.43, 95% CI 3.12 to 9.45; moderate-certainty evidence). However, these implants did not increase the risk of endophthalmitis, retinal tear, or retinal detachment (moderate-certainty evidence). In conclusion, the evidence suggests that corticosteroid implants may reduce the risk of uveitis recurrence compared to sham or standard-of-care therapy. However, their effects on visual acuity and quality of life are limited. These implants are associated with an increased risk of cataract progression and elevated IOP, which may require further interventions. Future studies are needed to better understand the efficacy and safety of corticosteroid implants, including different doses and durations of use, with standardized outcome measures and comparable follow-up periods.
